## Problem 1
```{r birthday-simulation, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
set.seed(8105)

has_shared_birthday <- function(group_size) {
  birthdays <- sample(1:365, size = group_size, replace = TRUE)
  any(duplicated(birthdays))
}

group_sizes <- 2:50
n_simulations <- 10000

birthday_results <- data.frame(
  group_size = group_sizes,
  probability = vapply(
    group_sizes,
    function(group_size) {
      mean(replicate(n_simulations, has_shared_birthday(group_size)))
    },
    numeric(1)
  )
)

plot(
  birthday_results$group_size,
  birthday_results$probability,
  type = "b",
  pch = 16,
  cex = 0.65,
  col = "steelblue",
  ylim = c(0, 1),
  xlab = "Group size",
  ylab = "Estimated probability",
  main = "Probability of at Least One Shared Birthday"
)
abline(h = 0.5, lty = 2, col = "gray50")
```

The estimated probability of at least one shared birthday increases with group size. At 23 people, the probability is approximately `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * birthday_results$probability[birthday_results$group_size == 23])`. By 50 people, it reaches approximately `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * birthday_results$probability[birthday_results$group_size == 50])`. Larger groups have more pairs of people who could share a birthday.

## Problem 2

```{r longitudinal-data, message=FALSE}
library(dplyr)
library(tidyr)
library(readr)
library(ggplot2)

longitudinal_data <- tibble(
  file_path = list.files(
    "data",
    pattern = "^(con|exp)_[0-9]+\\.csv$",
    full.names = TRUE
  )
) |>
  mutate(
    file_name = tools::file_path_sans_ext(basename(file_path)),
    measurements = purrr::map(
      file_path,
      read_csv,
      show_col_types = FALSE
    )
  ) |>
  select(file_name, measurements) |>
  separate_wider_delim(
    file_name,
    delim = "_",
    names = c("arm", "subject_id")
  ) |>
  unnest(measurements) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    names_transform = list(week = as.integer),
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    arm = recode(arm, con = "Control", exp = "Experimental")
  ) |>
  arrange(arm, subject_id, week)

knitr::kable(head(longitudinal_data))
```

```{r longitudinal-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(
  longitudinal_data,
  aes(
    x = week,
    y = observation,
    color = arm,
    group = interaction(arm, subject_id)
  )
) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 1.3, alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = sort(unique(longitudinal_data$week))) +
  labs(
    title = "Weekly Observations by Study Arm",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Study arm"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

Observations overlapped between the two arms in the first week. Over time, observations generally increased in the experimental arm, while those in the control arm fluctuated without a clear upward trend. The groups separated more clearly in the later weeks, with experimental participants generally showing higher observations.

## Problem 3

```{r t-test-simulation}
set.seed(8106)

simulate_t_test <- function(true_mu) {
  x <- rnorm(n = 30, mean = true_mu, sd = 5)

  t.test(x, mu = 0, alternative = "two.sided") |>
    broom::tidy() |>
    select(estimate, p.value)
}

t_test_results <- expand_grid(
  true_mu = 0:6,
  simulation = seq_len(5000)
) |>
  mutate(test_result = purrr::map(true_mu, simulate_t_test)) |>
  unnest(test_result) |>
  mutate(rejected = p.value < 0.05)

t_test_summary <- t_test_results |>
  group_by(true_mu) |>
  summarize(
    rejection_rate = mean(rejected),
    mean_estimate = mean(estimate),
    mean_estimate_rejected = mean(estimate[rejected]),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

```{r rejection-rate-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
ggplot(t_test_summary, aes(x = true_mu, y = rejection_rate)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.05, linetype = "dashed", color = "gray50") +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
  geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  scale_y_continuous(
    limits = c(0, 1),
    labels = scales::label_percent()
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Rejection Rate of the One-Sample t-Test",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Proportion of tests that reject the null"
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12)
```

When the true mean is zero, the estimated rejection rate is `r sprintf("%.1f%%", 100 * t_test_summary$rejection_rate[t_test_summary$true_mu == 0])`, close to the nominal 5% Type I error rate. For positive true means, power increases as the true mean moves farther from zero, approaching 100% at the largest effect sizes.

```{r mean-estimate-plot, fig.width=7, fig.height=4.5}
estimate_plot_data <- t_test_summary |>
  transmute(
    true_mu,
    `All samples` = mean_estimate,
    `Only samples that reject the null` = mean_estimate_rejected
  ) |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = -true_mu,
    names_to = "sample_set",
    values_to = "average_estimate"
  )

ggplot(
  estimate_plot_data,
  aes(x = true_mu, y = average_estimate, color = sample_set)
) +
  geom_abline(
    intercept = 0,
    slope = 1,
    linetype = "dashed",
    color = "gray50"
  ) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:6) +
  labs(
    title = "Average Estimated Mean vs. True Mean",
    x = "True mean",
    y = "Average estimated mean",
    color = NULL
  ) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

Across all simulated samples, the average estimated mean is close to the true mean. When the true mean is small and positive, averaging only the samples that reject the null tends to overestimate it. These samples are more likely to have estimates that are unusually high. As the true mean increases, nearly all tests reject the null, so the two averages converge. At a true mean of zero, the two-sided test selects extreme estimates in both directions, so their average can still be close to zero.
